tone_statements.citation: Doke, Clement M. 1931a. Report on the Unification of the Shona Dialects. Hertford: Stephen Austin & Sons (photographic reprint, ALLEX Project / Univ. of Zimbabwe & Univ. of Oslo, 2005, with intro by H. Chimhundu).
tone_statements.quote: 148. Significant Tone in Shona.—The Shona dialects, like almost every Bantu language, employ a varying of the pitch of the voice upon words to convey distinctive differences, This pitch alteration we term tone. Though there are several gradations of tone in Shona speech, it is found sufficient to indicate in scientific recording only three, a high tone, a mid tone, and a low tone. In ordinary speech these are all level tones, that is, upon any given syllable the musical note is maintained constant and does not glide from one position to another.

sources.citation: Chimhundu, Herbert. 2005. 'Doke and the development of Standard Shona', introduction to the ALLEX reprint of Doke 1931a (pp. 8-80 of the PDF text).
sources.note: Second-hand and about standard Shona, not Tawara: says Shona's word marker is 'penultimate length or stress' (after Fortune) and quotes the 1967 orthography commentary that the Shona spoken word carries 'an accent or prominence of extra length (and perhaps extra stress) on the second last syllable' which shifts as affixes are added (PDF text lines ~855-857, 2250-2258).

sources.note: Treats Tavara as a member of the Korekore Group (secs. 66-67, pp. 30-31; Northern Tavara in Tete is Nyungwe-influenced, Rhodesian Tavara Korekore-influenced); sec. 122 (p. 62) gives only Tavara consonantal peculiarities; the only stress remark is Shona-wide and generic, sec. 150 (p. 82): 'the function of stress in Bantu is that of word-building. In each word or word-group in Bantu there is one, and only one, main stress' — no statement of where it falls; Appendix IV vocabularies (incl. two Tavara lists) mark tone, not stress or length.
